payload.instructions: Preserve all candidate IDs and distinctions. Broader parent themes organize evidence; they do not imply measurement equivalence.

themes.disagreements: contradictions, weak signals, and proxy distinctions
evidence_ids: at most 12 representative supplied modeling evidence IDs
themes.name: theme

themes.disagreements: Rash/pruritus (285) shows robust prognostic and heterogeneity signals, while range of motion (283) and isolated rash (284) are weak; skeletal fractures (303) only show effect modification.
themes.interpretation: Cutaneous and skeletal manifestations show mixed utility, with combined skin measures being the most reliable signals.
themes.name: Dermatologic and Musculoskeletal Status

themes.disagreements: Smoking cessation duration (307) shows stronger treatment prediction than smoking status (306); biological sex and STK11 (302, 308) have moderate, mixed signals.
themes.interpretation: Patient demographics and tobacco history primarily serve as predictors for treatment assignment.
themes.name: Patient Demographics and Behavioral History

themes.disagreements: Tiotropium use (318) is a strong predictor of treatment and outcome, contrasting with fragmented or weak signals for TKI, NGS, and targeted therapy (315, 316, 320).
themes.interpretation: Prior medications and diagnostic tests show heterogeneous evidence, where specific agents (tiotropium) act as confounders and others as effect modifiers.
themes.name: Pharmacological and Diagnostic History

themes.disagreements: Strong effect modification signals in TTF1 and TMB contrast with weak signals for TP53 and tumor cell presence; TMB exhibits weaker treatment prediction than VAF.
themes.interpretation: Molecular and pathologic tumor markers showing a mixture of prognostic value, treatment selection bias, and significant effect modification.
themes.name: Tumor Molecular and Pathologic Characteristics

themes.disagreements: Ventricular edema (339) lacks treatment prediction support unlike vasogenic edema and hemorrhage; who_grade lacks strong effect modification compared to ventricular size and vertebral metastasis.
themes.interpretation: Indicators of neuro-oncological burden and imaging markers consistently linked to outcome prognosis and treatment selection, with some evidence of effect modification.
themes.name: Neuro-Oncological Imaging and Burden

themes.disagreements: Strong prognostic signals for transependymal flow and weight change contrast with weaker signals for bilirubin and ulceration; visual field deficit shows only effect modification.
themes.interpretation: Systemic clinical, hematologic, and physical findings reflecting patient health, serving as prognostic factors or effect modifiers.
themes.name: Systemic Clinical and Physiological Status

themes.disagreements: Robust effect modification for Vinorelbine and prior radiation/dosing (R-learner/causal forest) contrasts with the weak confounding role of vitamin supplements.
themes.interpretation: Prior pharmacological and therapeutic interventions exhibiting complementary signals for effect modification despite minimal evidence for main effects.
themes.name: Prior Therapeutic and Pharmacological History

themes.disagreements: Signals for treatment goals and response are fragmented across folds; thyromegaly presence shows negligible or inconsistent signaling across all roles.
themes.interpretation: Treatment-related documentation and clinical markers with insufficient evidence to be identified as stable confounders or modifiers.
themes.name: Treatment Documentation and Inconsistent Clinical Markers

themes.disagreements: Consistent evidence across univariable and predictive forest models for both treatment and outcome, with no significant effect modification signal.
themes.interpretation: Strong evidence of a common cause for both treatment assignment and outcome prognosis.
themes.name: Exposure-Related Confounding

system:
You review pretreatment candidate measurements using modeling evidence
from one outer-training fold. First identify themes across candidates; then
reconcile their roles as confounder, effect_modifier, both, or neither.
All evidence is fallible. No individual family, p-value, or support frequency is
a hard selection gate. A credible complementary signal can justify retention
even when other methods shrink it away. Do not mistake correlated aliases or
proxies for multiple independent discoveries. Themes organize evidence; they
do not establish equivalence, merge measurements, or transfer a role to every
theme member. Preserve investigator-locked roles exactly.

Treatment prediction, outcome prognosis, and confounding are distinct. Discuss
whether a candidate could be a common cause rather than an instrument or only a
prognostic factor. Effect modification needs treatment-heterogeneity evidence;
outcome main-effect importance alone does not establish it. Univariable logistic
interactions are on the log-odds scale and unadjusted for other covariates.
Orthogonal linear models, candidate R-learners, and causal forests assess the
probability/outcome scale after elastic-net nuisance adjustment. Their targets
and biases differ. A model family is evidence, not an independent replication.

Use exposure and evaluability denominators. Missing or nonconverged fits are not
negative votes. Repeated samples and folds overlap; support fractions are not
causal probabilities or formal stability-selection error guarantees. Raw and BH
p-values do not correct the upstream adaptive discovery process. Permutation
importance can be diluted by correlated alternatives and does not prove a
causal role. Compare fold consistency, methods, subsets, and conflicting facts.
Definitions and theme names cannot establish a role without the supplied
empirical evidence. Never invent an oracle, data-generating process, or hidden
truth. Return the requested JSON and cite only supplied evidence IDs.
